<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases and executed the pressure-question format cleanly, answering with proper A1/A2 labels. A's strongest moves were the Match Group rebuttal to the Hinge example, the exploitation of B's "ordered by prior engagement, not compatibility" concession, and the closing thesis that manipulated perception disables the exit-based market discipline B relies on. But B's case held up better under the final exchanges: B's "proxy, not corrupted signal" reframe blunted the engagement concession, and two of B's late rebuttals went unanswered by the end — that A's proposed regulatory proxies (ghosting rate, time-to-match) are themselves engagement metrics in disguise, and that A's proposed alternative revenue model (paid filters/likes) doesn't actually remove the "toll booth," just relabels it, undercutting the feasibility of PRO's remedy. B also used the genuine chronological last word (closing after A's closing) to directly rebut A's central "manipulated perception" punchline with the plausible counter-example of well-documented "swipe fatigue" and Tinder's paid-user decline, leaving A's final framing without a reply. The debate was close and both sides argued with discipline and no fabricated sourcing, but B ended with more live, unrebutted practical objections.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's late-round combo — reframing engagement-based ranking as an imperfect "proxy" rather than a corrupted signal, and showing that A's suggested regulatory proxies (ghosting/time-to-match) and alternative revenue model (paid filters/likes) are themselves engagement-flavored or a relabeled toll booth — landed as the most decisive, least-answered exchange of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
